title: Alberta vote on separation question begins Monday
excerpt: Albertans are voting on whether to keep Alberta in Canada or start the legal process for a later binding referendum on separation. Hand counting begins no earlier than 8 p.m. Monday.
body:
Hand counting on Alberta’s referendum ballot is set to begin no earlier than 8 p.m. local time Monday, with Question 10 to be tallied first as voters decide whether the province should stay in Canada or begin the legal process for a later binding referendum on separation, according to Elections Alberta.

The ballot question says: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?” Elections Alberta says the Oct. 19 vote itself is not binding, and that Question 10 will be counted first by hand.

Officials said results on the separation question should be available in the early hours of Tuesday. Questions 1 through 9 are also on the ballot, making 10 referendum questions in all.

Premier Danielle Smith called the vote earlier this year after a grassroots petition gathered about 300,000 signatures asking for a binding referendum on separation, BBC News reported. A separate petition opposing separation drew more than 400,000 signatures, according to BBC News.

Smith opposes separation and said on Oct. 14 that she had voted against seceding, Al Jazeera reported. The Alberta government says a court ruling found that a binding referendum on separation could not be held without a consultation process with First Nations on possible effects on treaty rights, and that the government is appealing that decision, according to the referendum materials from Albertareferendum2026.

Polling cited in the reports suggests many Albertans want to remain in Canada. Fox News reported that an Abacus Data poll involving 1,021 respondents released Saturday found that 74% of decided voters favored Alberta remaining within the Canadian Confederation, while 26% supported starting the process for a binding referendum on separation. Fox News also reported that a separate Angus Reid Institute poll of 1,010 Albertans released Friday found 62% believed “there will never be an end to the separatist movement” in the province.

Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to vote against separation at a rally in Edmonton on Thursday. Speaking there, he said, “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us,” BBC News reported.

Chris Scott, founder of the pro-separatist group Let’s Talk Alberta, told BBC News that the campaign had already achieved something important even if the separation side loses. “The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue,” he said. “What’s started can’t be stopped now,” he added.

BBC News also reported that Albertans in Edmonton over the weekend described feeling unheard in Ottawa, while opponents at a separate unity rally said they wanted to keep the country together.

issues.claim: "Hand counting on Alberta’s referendum ballot is set to begin no earlier than 8 p.m. local time Monday ... according to Elections Alberta."
issues.problem: The source excerpts do not show Elections Alberta as the source for the 8 p.m. start time. In the supplied excerpts, that timing comes from BBC News, while Elections Alberta supports that ballots are counted by hand and that Question 10 is counted first.
issues.fix: Attribute the 8 p.m. start time to BBC News, or remove "according to Elections Alberta" from the timing claim and keep Elections Alberta only for the hand count/Question 10 details.

issues.claim: The ballot question says: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”
issues.problem: This direct quotation is not verbatim. The source text includes a comma after "Canada".
issues.fix: Use the exact wording: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

issues.claim: "Officials said results on the separation question should be available in the early hours of Tuesday."
issues.problem: Attribution is vague. In the supplied excerpts, BBC News reports that officials said this, but the article does not identify the outlet or the officials.
issues.fix: Attribute specifically, e.g. "BBC News reported that officials said results on the separation question should be available in the early hours of Tuesday."

fc.summary: Two critical issues: the ballot question is misquoted, and the 8 p.m. count-start time is attributed to Elections Alberta though that detail is only supported here by BBC News. There is also one minor vague-attribution issue about who said results should be available early Tuesday.

originality.excerpt-repeats-lead: The excerpt and the opening paragraph repeat nearly the same sentences. Keep the central fact in both if needed, but open the article with a different verified detail or the next development instead of restating the excerpt.
originality.unrelated-ending: The last paragraph brings in a separate development the article does not connect to its subject ("BBC News also reported that Albertans in Edmonton over the weekend described fee…"). Keep background only if it explains the event, gives necessary context, clarifies a dispute, is a directly related development or shows consequences; otherwise remove it and end on the latest relevant verified development.

log.summary: Rewrote the preview as a straight news report using the supplied primary records and original reporting, removed unsupported material, and added the official counting timetable and ballot wording. Kept all facts anchored to sources available at the publication moment and separated the non-binding vote from any later process.
